title: The garland-maker (44–48)
hookLine: who will pick the well-taught path as a skilled hand picks flowers; death carries off the one still gathering
last: THE BODY LIKE A JAR — MORE THAN A MOTHER CAN.

cards: Walk past a temple in India, Sri Lanka or Thailand early in the morning and you'll see the garland-makers. They sit with baskets of jasmine, marigold, lotus, and their hands move fast: choosing, threading, knotting.
They don't take every flower. A skilled one can tell at a glance which bloom is fresh, which will last the day, which is already turning. Choosing well is the whole craft.
The fourth chapter of the Dhammapada opens at that basket.

teach.h: THE EARTH OUTSIDE, THE EARTH INSIDE.
teach.b: The commentary says a group of monks, back from a journey, sat talking about the ground they'd walked over: level here, muddy there, stony, rough. The Buddha told them: that's the earth outside.
Look at the earth inside you. And he spoke the chapter's first two verses. Who will master this earth, he asks, and the realms beyond it?

teach.h: PICK THE PATH LIKE THE RIGHT FLOWER.
teach.b: Who will pick out the well-taught path of the dhamma, the way a skilled garland-maker picks out the right flower? The one in training will. Not the one with the most flowers, but the one who can choose.
Verse forty-six adds that the body is like foam, like a mirage.
Then verse forty-seven, with a hard image: “Death carries off a man who is gathering flowers and whose mind is distracted, as a flood carries off a sleeping village.”

Gathering flowers, here, means collecting pleasures, one after another, never finished, never quite satisfied. Verse forty-eight says death takes that person “before he is satiated”, still reaching for the next bloom.
Side by side: one person gathers endlessly and never makes a garland; the other chooses carefully and makes something.
And this week you've been gathering well: appamada, heedfulness. An island. The racehorse, awake among the sleepers.
Citta and the fletcher. The gatekeeper. The jar.
The garland-maker's question is simpler: which one will you actually pick up and use?

how: Flower garlands are among the most common Buddhist offerings, and teachers use the chapter on flowers to encourage choosing one teaching to practice rather than collecting many.

o: one who chooses the right flower, as the wise pick the path
someone who collects as many blossoms as possible
a florist who sells flowers outside the temple gates

games.q: match the pictures in verses forty-four to forty-eight.

s: the garland-maker verse praises collecting as many flowers as possible
it praises choosing well: picking out the right flower, the well-taught path.
in the commentary, the monks had been talking about the roads they'd walked
the Buddha turned them from the earth outside to the earth inside.
verse forty-six compares the body to foam and a mirage

games.q: you've just come back from a long walk with your friends, and you're all comparing notes on the road: muddy here, rocky there. the Buddha joins you. what does he say?
o: tell me which road was best.
that's the earth outside; look at the earth inside.
you should have taken a cart.
games.why: in the commentary he turns their talk inward and speaks the first verses of the flower chapter.

practice: Picture the week's teachings laid out in a basket: heedful is alive, make an island, awake among the sleeping, straighten the arrow, guard the mind, more than a mother can.
Look them over like a garland-maker: which is fresh for you today, which fits the day you're about to have? Pick just one, let the others rest in the basket, and sit quietly with the one you chose.

wordCard.voice: The garland-maker. The skilled one who chooses the right flower from the basket, as the wise pick out the well-taught path.

orig.note: Pali: flower, the title of chapter four (Puppha Vagga).

carryVoice: Your line: pick the flower. One bloom, chosen well, from the whole basket. Day one hundred sixty-eight, done.

sources.q: Death carries off a man who is gathering flowers and whose mind is distracted, as a flood carries off a sleeping village.

sources.ref: Dhammapada 44–46; Dhammapada-atthakatha, story of the monks talking about the earth (verses 44–45)
